scope.included: Persistent, predominantly dry cough following an acute respiratory tract infection in adults.
excluded: cough in chronic lung disease other than asthma
diagnostic triage of the underlying cause

extractionLimitations: No full-text article was obtained for any source except king-2022-ajgp-viral-persistent-cough.
No effect sizes were extracted other than those quoted verbatim in retrieved summaries.
No risk-of-bias assessment was performed at study level.
No study design, sample size, comparator or outcome-timing table was built.
Certainty ratings below are the returning agent's provisional judgement, not GRADE assessments.

claims.statement: Cough that persists after a respiratory infection usually resolves without specific treatment, typically within eight weeks.
claims.population: adults following an acute respiratory tract infection

evidence.effectSummary: Subacute post-infectious cough is defined as lasting no more than eight weeks and resolving on its own.
evidence.rationale: Definitional and observational rather than experimental. The ACCP definition is nearly 20 years old; Australian duration data are from a single small primary-care series known here only at second hand.

caveats: Duration percentages at 3, 4, 6 and 8 weeks are NOT available in the literature located by this return.
Jones 2002 is an unverified secondary citation and must be obtained before any figure is published.

claims.statement: Over-the-counter cough mixtures have not been shown to relieve cough better than placebo.

evidence.effectSummary: Cochrane concluded there is no good evidence for or against effectiveness; Australian GP guidance states these mixtures have long failed to demonstrate benefit beyond placebo.
evidence.rationale: Cochrane evidence is limited by small, heterogeneous and poorly reported trials. Certainty downgraded for indirectness because the reviewed population is acute rather than subacute cough.

caveats: Population is acute cough; extension to post-infectious cough is indirect.
Cochrane review is from 2014 and may have been updated.

claims.statement: Dextromethorphan may produce a small reduction in cough symptoms in adults, but the clinical importance of that reduction is unclear.

intervention.name: dextromethorphan
intervention.regimenStudied: single 30 mg dose in the trials showing an effect

evidence.effectSummary: Some adult trials found a statistically significant reduction in cough counts, frequency, effort and intensity; others found no effect.
evidence.rationale: Direction is inconsistent across trials. NICE concluded the evidence was mixed and the clinical significance of any benefit unclear, with a possible increase in adverse effects.

caveats: Adverse effects reported include gastrointestinal upset and dizziness.
Serotonergic interaction risk requires pharmacist or medical advice; out of scope for this claim.
Evidence is for acute cough, not post-infectious cough.

claims.statement: Codeine has not been shown to reduce cough symptoms compared with placebo.

evidence.effectSummary: Cochrane found codeine no more effective than placebo; the NICE committee agreed codeine had no benefit on cough symptoms.
evidence.rationale: Consistent direction across two independent syntheses, but underlying trials are small and old.

caveats: Codeine is prescription-only in Australia; availability is a jurisdiction note, not a claim.
Harms of opioid antitussives were not extracted in this return.

claims.statement: Honey probably reduces cough frequency in children with acute cough compared with no treatment.
claims.population: children over 12 months with acute cough

evidence.effectSummary: Cochrane reported a mean difference of -1.05 (95% CI -1.48 to -0.62) on a 7-point Likert cough-frequency scale versus no treatment, I-squared 0%, 2 studies, 154 children.
evidence.rationale: Cochrane rated this comparison moderate certainty. Certainty is not downgraded further because the claim is stated only for the population actually studied.

caveats: Paediatric population only. This claim must NOT be restated as adult evidence.
Honey is contraindicated under 12 months of age - a separate safety item.
Most trials treated for a single night.

claims.statement: A honey and coffee preparation may reduce the severity of persistent post-infectious cough in adults.
claims.population: adults with post-infectious cough lasting more than three weeks

intervention.name: honey plus instant coffee
intervention.formulation: oral paste dissolved in warm water

evidence.effectSummary: A double-blind randomised trial in 97 adults reported honey plus coffee outperformed both prednisolone and guaifenesin control.
evidence.rationale: Downgraded heavily for very serious indirectness of setting, single research group, single centre, small sample, probable participant overlap with the same group's earlier reports, and a non-inert comparator.

caveats: Effect size was not extracted in this return; the full text has not been read.
Risk of bias has not been assessed.
Caffeine timing has sleep implications that are guidance, not evidence.
This is the only on-population adult trial located - do not present as a body of evidence.

claims.statement: Speech pathology cough-suppression therapy improves chronic cough that has persisted despite medical treatment.
claims.population: adults with chronic or refractory cough

evidence.effectSummary: A single-blind randomised placebo-controlled trial in 87 adults found significant improvement, replicated in a multicentre randomised trial and subsequently reviewed by Cochrane.
evidence.rationale: Two independent randomised trials with consistent direction plus a Cochrane review. Downgraded for indirectness: the studied population is refractory chronic cough, not subacute post-infectious cough.

caveats: Cochrane certainty ratings were NOT extracted; the stated certainty is provisional.
Trials delivered therapy by a trained clinician; self-directed technique is untested.
Applicability to cough under eight weeks is unestablished.

claims.statement: Inhaled corticosteroids have not been shown to produce a clinically important benefit for post-infectious cough in adults without asthma.
claims.population: adults with subacute post-infectious cough and no asthma

evidence.effectSummary: In a synthesis of mainly subacute cough (2 RCTs, 163 patients) inhaled corticosteroids showed a standardised mean difference of 0.42 versus placebo, against a placebo response of roughly 50-56% at two weeks; a wider review of six post-infectious cough RCTs found no clear patient-relevant benefit.
evidence.rationale: Small number of small trials with unclear or high risk of bias, and a very large placebo response that dominates the observed change.

caveats: CRITICAL SCOPE LIMIT: the underlying trials EXCLUDED people with asthma. This claim must never be presented to, or about, people with asthma.
The OSPIC source is a protocol; its published results must be located.
Bronchodilator and combination bronchodilator claims were not separately extracted.

claims.statement: Acid-suppressing medicines alone are unlikely to resolve cough in people who have no heartburn or regurgitation.
claims.population: adults with chronic cough and no reflux symptoms

evidence.effectSummary: ACCP guidance advises that proton pump inhibitors alone are not likely to resolve cough and should not be prescribed without accompanying lifestyle modification; Australian chronic cough guidance discourages their use where reflux symptoms are absent.
evidence.rationale: Guideline recommendations rest on low-quality evidence, but two independent guideline bodies agree on direction.

caveats: The AFP article is a summary; the primary CHEST guideline must be cited directly.
The Lung Foundation source is a landing-page description; the PDF itself has not been read.
Non-drug reflux measures are separate and rated separately.

claims.statement: Saline nasal irrigation may help symptoms after an upper respiratory infection, but the evidence is weak.
claims.population: adults and children after an upper respiratory tract infection

evidence.effectSummary: Australian guidance describes possible benefit for acute URTI symptoms while noting included trials were generally small and at high risk of bias.
evidence.rationale: Very low certainty from small, high-risk-of-bias trials. Included here because upper airway cough syndrome is described as the most common explanation for post-viral cough.

caveats: The underlying Cochrane review (CD006821) was NOT read in this return.
Cough was not the primary outcome of the underlying trials.
Water-safety instructions are a safety item, not part of this claim.

claims.statement: Steam inhalation has not been shown to shorten upper respiratory infections.
claims.population: adults with an upper respiratory tract infection

evidence.effectSummary: Australian guidance states there is no reliable evidence that steam inhalation reduces the duration of upper respiratory infections.
evidence.rationale: Single narrative-review source with onward citation; underlying trials not examined in this return.

caveats: Comfort effects are not the same as duration effects and are not assessed here.
Scald risk is a separate safety item and is not covered by this claim.

claims.statement: There is no randomised trial evidence that drinking more fluid than thirst dictates helps acute respiratory infections.
claims.population: adults with an acute respiratory tract infection

evidence.effectSummary: Australian guidance states there is no randomised controlled trial evidence to recommend increased fluid intake for acute respiratory infections.
evidence.rationale: Absence of evidence rather than evidence of absence; the underlying Cochrane review reported no eligible trials.

caveats: Absence of trial evidence must not be presented to readers as evidence of harm or of no effect.
Normal hydration advice is unaffected by this claim.
